Carpal injuries

Normal anatomy of the carpus

Carpal Injuries

Carpal injuries include

  • Simple self-limiting sprains of the joint capsule and interosseous ligaments (Dx of exclusion)
  • More serious unstable tears of the joint capsule and interosseous ligaments
  • Carpal bones fractures: scaphoid (most common), triquetrum …
  • Carpal dislocations: lunate and peri lunate dislocations …

Surface anatomy

Demonstration on my hand

Normal anatomy: ligaments

Henry Vandyke Carter, Public domain, via Wikimedia Commons

Triangular fibrocartilage complex is a load bearing structure between the ulnar head, lunate and triquetrum , it act as a stabilizer of the ulnar side of the wrist

TFCC is composed of:

Triangular fibrocartilage disc

Extensor carpi ulnaris tendon sub sheath

Ulnotriquetral and ulnolunate ligaments

Ulnocarpal collateral ligament

Radioulnar ligament

Elatmani s, CC BY-SA 3.0 <https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by-sa/3.0>, via Wikimedia Commons

TFCC tear

TFCC can get injured in forced ulnar deviation in baseball players or when swinging a rachet

Risk factors for TFCC tear is positive ulnar variance (ulna is longer than radius so the articular surface of ulna is more distal than articular surface of radius) and that occur due to prior surgery or prior fracture

Iiibalesiii, CC BY-SA 4.0 <https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by-sa/4.0>, via Wikimedia Commons

Patient present as ulnar sided wrist pain and maybe clicking or point tenderness between the pisiform and the ulnar head, ulnar deviation reproduces symptoms (TFCC compression test), applying a force across the ulna with the wrist in ulnar deviation reproduces symptoms (press test)

Injurymap, CC BY 4.0 <https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by/4.0>, via Wikimedia Commons

Diagnosed by MRI and arthrography

Treatment is either conservative (rest, NSAIDs, corticosteroid injections) or operative

Operative management indicated if conservative treatment failed or if there is DRUJ instability

Clinical features

Symptoms

Patient present with wrist pain and they report some type of injury mechanism like falling on the outstretched hand, or getting hit by some type of object

InjuryMap, CC BY-SA 4.0 <https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by-sa/4.0>, via Wikimedia Commons

Physical examination

Look

Look for Swelling, contusions and lacerations

Deformity maybe seen (in dislocation)

Inspect the lacerations for any evidence of open fracture

Feel

Feel for tenderness over the forearm, wrist and hand

Neurovascular examination is done to look for nerve/vessel injury, inquire about weakness, numbness, paresthesia and motor examination

Physical examination

Tenderness should be carefully localized (blunt end of a pencil is useful for testing for point tenderness)

When the scapholunate ligament is injured => tenderness is present just beyond Lister’s tubercle

for lunate dislocation => in the middle of the wrist

for triquetral injuries => beyond the head of the ulna

for hamate fractures => at the base of the hypothenar eminence

for TFCC injuries => over the dorsum of the ulnocarpal joint.

https://www.scientificanimations.com, CC BY-SA 4.0 <https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by-sa/4.0>, via Wikimedia Commons

Physical examination

Move

Movements are often limited (more by pain than by stiffness) and they may be accompanied by a palpable or an audible clunk.

If patient have a good range of active movement on their wrist joint then injury is most likely mild

Imaging

X-rays are the first line investigation modality for carpal injuries

Initially, four standard views are obtained:

PA with wrist in ulnar deviation

Lateral

Semi-pronated oblique

Semi-supinated oblique.

An AP view with the ﬁst clenched is added when the space between the scaphoid and lunate is increased on initial x rays (scapholunate injury).

If the initial X-rays are ‘normal’, treat the clinical diagnosis and immobilize the wrist. 10–15% of scaphoid fractures are not visible on initial X-rays.

Early MRI is very helpful in detecting capsule, ligaments and tendon injuries and confirms fracture diagnosis but If MRI is not available, repeated X-rays are needed 2 weeks later (bone resorption and movement can make the fracture more apparent). If there is still doubt then x ray repeated after another 2 weeks

In the anteroposterior X-ray note the shape of the carpus, whether the individual bones are clearly outlined and whether there are any abnormally large gaps suggesting disruption of the ligaments.

The scaphoid may be fractured; or it may have lost its normal bean shape and look squat and foreshortened, sometimes with an inner circular density (the cortical ring sign) – features of an end-on view when the bone is hyperﬂexed because of damage to the restraining scapholunate ligament. The lunate is normally quadrilateral in shape but, if it is dislocated, it looks triangular.

Mikael Häggström, M.D., CC0, via Wikimedia Commons
Mohamed Jarraya, Daichi Hayashi, Frank W. Roemer, Michel D. Crema, Luis Diaz, Jane Conlin, Monica D. Marra, Nabil Jomaah, and Ali Guermazi, CC BY 3.0 <https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by/3.0>, via Wikimedia Commons

In the lateral X-ray the axes of the radius, lunate, capitate and third metacarpal are co-linear, and the scaphoid projects at an angle of about 45 degrees to this line. With traumatic instability the linked carpal segments collapse (like the buckled carriages of a derailed train). Two patterns are recognized: dorsal intercalated segment instability (DISI), in which the lunate is torn from the scaphoid and tilted backwards; and volar intercalated segment instability (VISI), in which the lunate is torn from the triquetrum and turns towards the palm; the capitate shows a complementary dorsal tilt. There may be a ﬂake fracture off the back of a carpal bone (usually the triquetrum) that indicates avulsion of the dorsal radiocarpal ligament.

Mikael Häggström, CC0, via Wikimedia Commons · James Heilman, MD, CC BY-SA 3.0 <https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by-sa/3.0>, via Wikimedia Commons

MRI can miss TFCC tears and interosseous ligament tears sometimes

Arthrography is used to look for these injuries

Bone scan will exclude injury if negative but it is not specific if positive

Arthroscopy is helpful in detecting scapholunate or lunotriquetral ligament injuries

Management

‘Wrist sprain’ is a diagnosis of exclusion, when a more serious injury has been excluded with certainty, in serious injuries there is limitation to wrist movement.

Even with apparently trivial injuries, ligaments might be torn and patient may develop carpal instability later.

If the x-ray is normal and clinical picture highly suggest an injury, then immobilize the wrist and request further investigations to look for the injury

immobilization is done with below elbow backslab

Slide 30

The aim is to treat as soon as possible if there is an injury, or to avoid an unnecessary period of immobilization and time from work. If these tests are not readily available, the patient should be re-examined repeatedly until the symptoms settle or a ﬁrm diagnosis is made.
